blocks.text: 1. Image Representation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445339591-608024974.png

Hyperband, the final topic of the previous Hyperparameter Tuning module, closed out that module's coverage of search strategies. Image Representation opens the Convolutional Neural Networks module, shifting focus to a genuinely new kind of data entirely.

It covers how an image actually becomes numbers a network can process, a genuinely foundational prerequisite covered in full depth throughout this topic, and assumed by every subsequent topic in this module.
2. Pixels As A Grid Of Numbers

blocks.alt: Pixels As A Grid Of Numbers
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445339591-39444229.png

The genuinely core, foundational idea underlying this entire topic is that an image is genuinely just a grid of numbers, arranged in rows and columns, no different in kind from any other numeric data already covered throughout this course.
Each individual number is called a pixel, the smallest unit of that grid, and every single visual detail in an image ultimately reduces to these individual pixel values.
3. Grayscale Image Representation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445339828-125591718.png
This connects back to a single grid of numbers, already covered in this topic. A grayscale image needs just one such grid, since it only carries brightness information, no color at all.
Each pixel value represents brightness, typically ranging from 0, black, to 255, white, with everything in between representing some intermediate shade of gray.

blocks.text: 4. Color Image Representation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445339830-614853467.png

This connects back to Instance Normalization's own channel concept, already covered in the Normalization Techniques module. A color image needs three separate grids, or channels: red, green, and blue.

Stacked together, these three channels genuinely represent the full color image, with each pixel location now holding three separate numeric values instead of the single value already covered for grayscale images.
5. The Image Shape Convention

A genuinely important, real practical convention describes an image's shape as height times width times channels, a compact way of capturing all three dimensions already covered in the previous two sections.
This is a genuinely standard way to describe image dimensions throughout this entire module, used consistently across every topic covering convolutions, pooling, and feature maps still to come.
6. Normalizing Pixel Values
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445339831-341426958.png

This connects back to Feature Scaling, already covered in the Normalization Techniques module. Raw pixel values, typically 0 to 255, commonly get rescaled to a smaller range, like 0 to 1, before training.
This uses the exact same standardization or min-max scaling ideas already covered there, applied here to images, keeping pixel values in a genuinely consistent, well-behaved range for training.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Skipping pixel normalization is a genuinely common, real mistake for newcomers. Unnormalized pixel values, already covered in this topic, can slow down or destabilize training the same way any unscaled feature could, already covered in Feature Scaling.

blocks.text: 7. Why Fully Connected Layers Genuinely Struggle Here

blocks.alt: Why Fully Connected Layers Genuinely Struggle Here
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445339831-903510115.png

A genuinely important motivating problem follows. This connects back to fully connected layers, already covered in Network Architecture. Flattening a genuinely large image into one giant vector loses spatial structure entirely.
A single, genuinely large image can also produce an enormous number of individual pixel values, making a fully connected layer processing all of them directly genuinely impractical at real scale.
8. Why Spatial Structure Genuinely Matters
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445339832-435455545.png
A genuinely important insight follows directly from the previous section. Nearby pixels in an image are genuinely, meaningfully related to each other, forming edges, textures, and shapes together.

A network that respects this spatial structure, covered in the very next topic of this module, can learn far more efficiently than one that treats every pixel as a genuinely independent, unrelated input.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing Why This Foundational Representation Genuinely Matters
This connects back to every Convolutional Neural Network topic covered throughout the rest of this module. Every one of them builds directly on this pixel-grid representation already covered here.

Preprocessing real image data before training is another genuine case where correctly representing images as numbers, already covered in this topic, is the genuinely essential first step before anything else can happen.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates representing both a grayscale and a color image as numeric grids, and normalizing their pixel values, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)

# A genuinely small grayscale image, already covered in this topic
grayscale_image = rng.randint(0, 256, size=(4, 4))
print("Grayscale image shape (height, width):", grayscale_image.shape)
print("Grayscale image:\n", grayscale_image)

# A genuinely small color image, already covered as needing three channels in this topic
color_image = rng.randint(0, 256, size=(4, 4, 3))
print("\nColor image shape (height, width, channels), already covered as the shape convention:", color_image.shape)

# Normalizing pixel values, already covered in this topic
normalized_color_image = color_image / 255.0
print("\nNormalized color image range:", normalized_color_image.min(), "to", normalized_color_image.max())

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the grayscale image's shape has just two dimensions while the color image's shape has three, exactly the channel distinction already covered in this topic between grayscale and color representation.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: An image is fundamentally a grid of numbers, with each number called a pixel.
A grayscale image needs one grid, encoding brightness from 0 to 255.
A color image needs three grids, or channels, for red, green, and blue.
An image's shape is commonly written as height times width times channels.
Pixel values commonly get rescaled from 0 to 255 down to a smaller range like 0 to 1.
Flattening images into one giant vector for a fully connected layer loses spatial structure.
Nearby pixels are meaningfully related, motivating architectures that respect this structure.
Next up: The Convolution Operation, the foundational computation that respects this spatial structure directly.
